The circuit is an **OR** feeding an **AND**, so Y = (A + B)·C.
**Step 1 — write the output.**
Y = **(A + B) · C** ✓
**Step 2 — see what Y = 1 requires.** An AND gives 1 only when **both** its inputs are
1, so
**C = 1** ✓ and **A + B = 1** ✓
and the OR gives 1 when **at least one** of A and B is 1.
**Step 3 — test the options.**
**0, 1, 0**: C = 0 ✗ the AND gives 0 whatever the OR does
**1, 0, 0**: C = 0 ✗ same objection
**1, 0, 1**: A + B = 1 ✓ and C = 1 ✓ so **Y = 1** ✓
**1, 1, 0**: C = 0 ✗
**Step 4 — conclude.** Only **1, 0, 1** works ✓
**The quickest route.** Check **C** first ✓ The AND gate makes C a veto: if C = 0 the
output is 0 regardless of A and B. That single test eliminates three of the four
options at once, without looking at the OR gate at all.
**The full truth table.** Y = 1 for
(0, 1, 1), (1, 0, 1) and (1, 1, 1) ✓
three of the eight input combinations - those with C = 1 and at least one of A, B set.
**Why gates are read right to left.** The **final** gate determines what the output
requires ✓ Working backwards from it to the inputs is almost always faster than
evaluating forwards.
**The Boolean expansion.**
Y = (A + B)C = **AC + BC** ✓ by the distributive law - which shows the same thing: C
must be 1, and one of A or B with it.
**Where such a circuit is used.** C acts as an **enable** line ✓ The OR combines two
signals, and C decides whether the result is passed on. This is the basic structure of
a gated logic block, and of the enable inputs on every memory chip.
**Why the OR gate alone is not enough.** It would give Y = 1 for A = 1 regardless of C ✓
The AND adds the condition, and the question is really about understanding that
combination.
**Reading the distractors.** Each of the other three has **C = 0** ✓ and no value of A
and B can rescue an AND gate with a zero input.
∴ 1, 0, 1.

Trailing zeros **after a decimal point** count; so do zeros **between** significant
digits.
**Step 1 — count in 4·8000 x 10⁴.** The power of ten plays no part - only the
**mantissa** matters:
4, 8, 0, 0, 0 → **5 significant figures** ✓
The trailing zeros are written **deliberately** after the decimal point to show the
precision, so they count.
**Step 2 — count in 48000·50.**
4, 8, 0, 0, 0, 5, 0 → **7 significant figures** ✓
Every digit counts here: the three middle zeros lie **between** significant digits, and
the final zero follows a decimal point.
**Step 3 — state the pair.** **5 and 7** ✓
**The rules, set out.**
all **non-zero** digits count ✓
zeros **between** non-zero digits always count ✓
**leading** zeros never count - 0·0045 has **2** ✓
**trailing** zeros count **only if a decimal point is present** ✓
**Why the ambiguity of 48000.** Without a decimal point it could be 2, 3, 4 or 5
significant figures ✓ Writing it as 4·8 x 10⁴ or 4·8000 x 10⁴ removes the doubt
entirely - which is precisely why scientific notation is preferred in careful work.
**Why 48000·50 is unambiguous.** The decimal point settles it ✓ Every digit shown is
claimed to be known, including the final zero in the hundredths place.
**What significant figures mean physically.** They record how precisely a quantity was
**measured** ✓ 4·8000 x 10⁴ claims a measurement to one part in 48000; 4·8 x 10⁴ claims
only one part in 48.
**Why trailing zeros after the point are never idle.** Writing them is a deliberate
claim ✓ Nobody writes 4·8000 unless the last two zeros were actually measured.
**The rules for calculations.**
**multiplication and division**: keep the fewest **significant figures** ✓
**addition and subtraction**: keep the fewest **decimal places** ✓
Two different rules, and mixing them is the usual error.
**Reading the distractors.** **2 and 7** ✗ and **2 and 6** ✗ discount the trailing
zeros in the first number. **5 and 6** ✗ miscounts the second ✓
∴ 5 and 7.

The rating gives the power at the stated voltage, so **I = P/V**.
**Step 1 — write the relation.** A heater is purely **resistive**, so the power factor
is 1 and
P = VI ✓
**Step 2 — solve for the current.**
I = P/V
= 550/220
= **2·5 A** ✓
**Why the power factor is 1.** A heating element has negligible inductance and
capacitance ✓ so the current is in **phase** with the voltage, and the simple product
VI gives the average power. For a motor or a fluorescent lamp one would need
P = VI cos φ.
**What the rating means.** "220 V, 550 W" states the power the heater draws **when
supplied at 220 V** ✓ Connect it to a lower voltage and both the current and the power
fall.
**The element's resistance.**
R = V²/P = (220)²/550 = **88 Ω** ✓
and a check: I = V/R = 220/88 = **2·5 A** ✓
**What happens on a 110 V supply.** The resistance is fixed, so
I = 110/88 = **1·25 A** and P = **137·5 W** ✓ one **quarter** of the rated power, since
P ∝ V². That quadratic dependence is why appliances perform so poorly on a low mains
voltage.
**Why the values are rms.** A.c. ratings always use **rms** values ✓ which are defined
precisely so that P = VI and P = I²R work exactly as for direct current. The peak
current here is 2·5√2 = **3·54 A**.
**The fuse needed.** A **5 A** fuse ✓ comfortably above the 2·5 A working current but
well below the cable's rating - the standard choice for a 550 W appliance.
**The energy consumed.** Running for 2 hours:
E = 0·55 kW x 2 h = **1·1 kWh** ✓ about one unit on the electricity bill.
**Why resistance rises in use.** A hot element has a higher resistance than a cold
one ✓ so the switch-on current briefly exceeds 2·5 A. The rating refers to the working
condition.
**Reading the distractors.** **1·25 A** ✗ is the current at 110 V. **0·4 A** ✗ and
**0·8 A** ✗ correspond to powers of 88 W and 176 W ✓ The division 550/220 is the whole
of it.
∴ 2.5 A.

Mixing two quantities of the same liquid gives a **volume-weighted average** of the
temperatures.
**Step 1 — note what cancels.** Both samples are water, so they share the same density
and specific heat ✓ The masses are therefore proportional to the **volumes**.
**Step 2 — write the heat balance.** Heat lost by the hot equals heat gained by the
cold:
0·1(80 − T) = 0·3(T − 60) ✓
**Step 3 — expand and solve.**
8 − 0·1T = 0·3T − 18
26 = 0·4T
**T = 65 °C** ✓
**The weighted-average shortcut.**
T = (V₁T₁ + V₂T₂)/(V₁ + V₂) ✓
= [0·1(80) + 0·3(60)]/0·4
= (8 + 18)/0·4
= **65 °C** ✓ in one line.
**Why the answer lies nearer 60 than 80.** There is **three times** as much cold water ✓
so the mixture settles much closer to the cold temperature - a quarter of the way up
from 60 to 80, that is 60 + 5 = **65 °C**.
**The energy check.**
hot water loses 100 kg x 4200 x 15 = **6·3 MJ**
cold water gains 300 kg x 4200 x 5 = **6·3 MJ** ✓ equal, as they must be.
**Why the specific heat never appears.** It is the same for both and cancels ✓ Had the
liquids been **different** - water and oil, say - their specific heats would have to be
kept, and the weighting would be by **mc** rather than by volume alone.
**The bounds that check the answer.** T must lie strictly **between 60 and 80** ✓ and
**below 70**, the unweighted mean, since cold water predominates. Only 65 satisfies
both - a check worth making before any arithmetic.
**The assumptions.** No heat lost to the container or surroundings, and no change of
state ✓ A real calorimeter experiment must allow for the vessel's own heat capacity.
**Reading the distractors.** **70 °C** ✗ is the **unweighted** mean, right only for
equal volumes - and it is the designed trap. **60 °C** ✗ would need the hot water to
contribute nothing, and **75 °C** ✗ lies above the midpoint, which would need **more**
hot water than cold ✓
∴ 65 °C.

A planet moves **fastest at perihelion**, the point of **closest approach** to the Sun.
**Step 1 — apply Kepler's second law.** The radius vector sweeps **equal areas in equal
times** ✓ so when the planet is **close** to the Sun, the short radius must be
compensated by a **large** speed.
**Step 2 — read the figure.** The Sun sits at the focus nearer **A** ✓ so A is the
**perihelion** - the nearest point - and the planet's speed is **greatest there**.
**Step 3 — conclude.** The linear speed is maximum at **A** ✓
**The conservation law behind it.** Gravity is a **central** force, always directed at
the Sun, so it exerts **no torque** about the Sun ✓ Angular momentum
L = mvr is therefore constant, and
**v ∝ 1/r** at the two apses - the closer the point, the faster the planet.
**The energy view.** Approaching the Sun, the planet **loses** gravitational potential
energy and **gains** kinetic energy ✓
½mv² − GMm/r = constant ✓
Smallest r means largest v.
**The Earth's own case.** Perihelion is in early **January**, at 147 million km, where
the Earth moves at **30·3 km s⁻¹** ✓ Aphelion is in July, at 152 million km and
**29·3 km s⁻¹** - a 3% variation, which is why the seasons are of unequal length.
**Why the orbit is an ellipse at all.** Kepler's **first** law, and it follows from the
**inverse-square** nature of gravity ✓ Any other power law would give a non-closing
orbit.
**Where C lies.** At the far end of the major axis - the **aphelion** ✓ where the planet
is slowest. B and D lie at the ends of the minor axis, at intermediate distances and
speeds.
**The third law, for completeness.** T² ∝ a³ ✓ relating the **period** to the semi-major
axis - the law from which planetary distances were first deduced.
**Why comets show the effect so dramatically.** A highly eccentric orbit means a huge
range of r ✓ Halley's comet travels at 54 km s⁻¹ at perihelion and under 1 km s⁻¹ at
aphelion, spending most of its 76 years crawling through the outer solar system.
**Reading the distractors.** **C** ✗ is the aphelion, where the speed is **least**.
**B** and **D** ✗ are intermediate points on the minor axis ✓
∴ A.

A star's surface temperature is found from the **colour** at which it radiates most -
**Wien's displacement law**.
**Step 1 — state the law.**
**λ_max T = b = 2·9 x 10⁻³ m K** ✓
**Step 2 — see how it is used.** Measure the wavelength at which the star's spectrum
peaks, and the temperature follows at once:
T = **2·9 x 10⁻³/λ_max** ✓
**Worked examples.**
the **Sun**, peaking at 500 nm: T = 2·9 x 10⁻³/5 x 10⁻⁷ = **5800 K** ✓
**Betelgeuse**, peaking at 830 nm: **3500 K** - red ✓
**Rigel**, peaking at 260 nm: **11000 K** - blue-white ✓
**Why colour is a thermometer.** Hotter bodies peak at **shorter** wavelengths ✓ so the
sequence red - orange - yellow - white - blue is a sequence of **increasing**
temperature. A blue star is hotter than a red one, contrary to everyday colour
associations.
**Why this is the only practical method.** One cannot visit a star ✓ Its light is all
there is, and Wien's law converts its colour into a temperature directly. In practice
astronomers measure the brightness through two filters and use the **colour index**
B − V, which amounts to the same thing.
**The companion law.** **Stefan's law**, P = σAT⁴, gives the **total** power ✓ Combined
with Wien's, and with the distance, it yields the star's **radius** - which is how we
know Betelgeuse is a thousand times the Sun's diameter.
**Why not the other laws.**
**Rayleigh-Jeans** ✗ is the **classical** approximation, valid only at long wavelengths;
at short ones it diverges - the ultraviolet catastrophe.
**Planck's law** ✗ gives the **full** spectral distribution, and Wien's law is derived
**from** it by differentiation ✓ It is correct but not the practical tool for a quick
temperature.
**Kirchhoff's law** ✗ relates emissivity to absorptivity, and explains the **dark
lines** in a stellar spectrum rather than the temperature.
**How the law was found.** Wien derived it in 1893 from thermodynamics, before Planck's
quantum theory ✓ and received the 1911 Nobel Prize for his work on heat radiation.
**The everyday version.** A heated poker glows dull red, then orange, then
yellow-white ✓ the peak marching towards the blue exactly as λ_max = b/T requires.
∴ Wein's displacement law.

A **continuous** spectrum comes from a hot **dense** source - an incandescent filament.
**Step 1 — recall the condition.** Continuous emission requires a **hot solid, liquid
or dense gas** ✓ There the atoms are so close together that their energy levels are
smeared out by constant interaction, and radiation of **every** wavelength is emitted.
**Step 2 — examine the options.**
**incandescent lamp** ✓ a tungsten **filament** at about 2800 K - a hot **solid**,
giving a continuous spectrum
**mercury vapour lamp** ✗ a rarefied gas discharge - **line** emission, which is why
its light is harsh and bluish
**sodium vapour lamp** ✗ also line emission, dominated by the two yellow **D lines** at
589 nm - the reason street lighting renders colours so poorly
**the Sun** ✗ its photosphere does emit a continuum, but the overlying cooler gases
impose dark **Fraunhofer** lines, so the observed spectrum is a **line absorption**
one ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** The **incandescent electric lamp** ✓
**Why the Sun is the subtle distractor.** Its **underlying** spectrum is continuous ✓
but what reaches us is crossed by thousands of absorption lines, so the spectrum as
**observed** is not continuous. The question asks what **produces** a continuous
spectrum, and only the filament does so cleanly.
**Why a dense source gives a continuum.** Atoms packed together perturb one another's
energy levels constantly ✓ The sharp levels of an isolated atom broaden and overlap
until every wavelength becomes possible.
**Why a rarefied gas gives lines.** Its atoms are far apart and essentially
undisturbed ✓ so their levels stay sharp and only certain transitions - hence certain
wavelengths - occur.
**The filament's spectrum in detail.** Approximately black-body at 2800 K, peaking by
Wien's law at
λ_max = 2·9 x 10⁻³/2800 = **1·04 µm** ✓ in the **infrared** - which is why an
incandescent lamp is only about 5% efficient as a source of light, and why it is so
warm.
**Why this matters for colour rendering.** A continuous spectrum contains **all**
wavelengths, so colours appear natural ✓ A sodium lamp, having only two, makes
everything look yellow or grey - which is why incandescent and full-spectrum LED
lighting is preferred where colour matters.
∴ Incandescent electric lamp.
